title: Ohio's Implementation of the Science of Reading
author: Aaron Churchill
summary: Aaron Churchill summarizes a new Fordham Institute report assessing Ohio's implementation of two landmark literacy reforms, the 2012 third grade reading guarantee and the 2023 science-of-reading initiative, against a backdrop of NAEP scores showing 38 percent of Ohio fourth graders and 31 percent of eighth graders reading 'below basic,' the worst levels since the turn of the century. The report finds genuinely mixed results: on curriculum and teacher preparation, Ohio has made real, documented progress, banning non-scientifically based reading programs, adopting Core Knowledge Language Arts as the state's most-used K-5 core curriculum, training over 115,000 educators, placing reading coaches in 151 low-performing schools, and auditing teacher-prep programs (with 10 of 48 failing and given 12 months to correct or close). But on accountability, the reforms have been substantially undermined: state lawmakers weakened the third grade retention requirement in 2023 to allow parental-request promotion, and the resulting 'social promotion' saw 98 percent of third graders advance to fourth grade in 2024-25 despite only 61 percent statewide reading proficiency, with 21,658 students promoted specifically through the parental loophole. Churchill's recommendations for sustaining momentum center on restoring the retention requirement, requiring more frequent parent meetings for struggling readers, strengthening teacher-prep audits, and shifting curriculum focus beyond phonics toward vocabulary and background knowledge, since just over half of Ohio districts still use third-grade reading programs of 'questionable depth' on those dimensions.
points: The report's starkest finding is the disconnect between proficiency and promotion: 98 percent of Ohio third graders were promoted to fourth grade in 2024-25 despite only 61 percent achieving state reading proficiency, with 21,658 students specifically promoted through a 2023-created parental-override loophole.

Ohio's teacher-preparation audit produced a concrete accountability result: 10 of 48 colleges of education, including both Ohio University and Ohio State University, failed alignment audits and now have 12 months to correct or face program closure.

On curriculum quality, the report documents that Core Knowledge Language Arts, a knowledge-rich program, became Ohio's most-used K-5 core reading curriculum in 2024-25, evidence that state curriculum bans on non-scientific programs are producing measurable adoption shifts, not just policy language.

Churchill flags an under-discussed implementation gap: just over half of Ohio districts use third-grade reading curricula of 'questionable depth' in vocabulary and background-knowledge instruction, arguing science-of-reading discourse over-indexes on phonics relative to the comprehension-supporting knowledge pillars.

His policy prescription is explicitly sequenced around a leadership transition risk: with Governor DeWine's term-limited tenure ending, he argues sustained gubernatorial commitment to literacy reform, not just the existing statutory framework, is necessary to keep the state's implementation from stalling or reversing.
quotes: Approximately half of American adults read at a sixth-grade level or below, according to the Barbara Bush Foundation.
In Ohio, 38 percent of fourth graders and 31 percent of eighth graders scored "below basic" on the most recent National Assessment of Educational Progress.
Ohio unfortunately gutted the retention requirement: state lawmakers in 2023 weakened the guarantee's retention provision by allowing schools to promote struggling students based on parental request.

In 2024-25, 98 percent of third graders were promoted despite a statewide third grade reading proficiency rate of just 61 percent. Of the grade-promoted students, 21,658 students advanced to fourth grade through the parental loophole.

By the end of 2025, a large majority of Ohio classroom teachers, reading specialists, and administrators, more than 115,000 educators in all, completed an introductory professional development (PD) course in the science of reading.
Thirty-eight out of 48 programs were deemed in full or partial alignment but 10 failed the audit, including Ohio University and Ohio State University.
Literacy has the power to change lives. It can unlock further education and rewarding careers. It opens minds to new ideas and ways of thinking.
